name: AHK-Cu

lead: AHK-Cu is a copper-bound three-amino-acid peptide (alanyl-histidyl-lysine, copper tripeptide-3) sold in hair-care products and related to the better-known GHK-Cu. People use it hoping for a longer hair growth phase, thicker hairs and a fuller scalp.

In a laboratory study on cultured human hair follicle cells, a tripeptide-copper complex was reported to boost fibroblast growth and VEGF and to act on dermal papilla cells, the cells that steer hair follicle growth. No human hair-growth trial of AHK-Cu was found.

paras: It is used as a topical ingredient in scalp serums and hair-care products, usually as part of a regular routine alongside other hair treatments.
No human safety or efficacy data specific to AHK-Cu were found.

angle.text: AHK-Cu is a copper tripeptide marketed in hair-care products and discussed as a hair-growth ingredient, much as GHK-Cu is for skin. It is thought to act on follicle cells for a longer growth phase and thicker hairs. Published work so far is a cell-culture study.

lead: AHK-Cu is a copper complex of the tripeptide alanyl-histidyl-lysine, also called copper tripeptide-3. It is marketed in hair-care products and discussed in appearance circles as a hair-growth ingredient, with the aim of keeping or thickening hair on the scalp so the hairline and density look fuller, in the way the related GHK-Cu is discussed for skin and hair.[1][2]

The published research is a 2007 study in Archives of Pharmacal Research in which AHK-Cu at very low concentrations (10 to the minus 12 to minus 9 molar) stimulated elongation of human hair follicles ex vivo and proliferation of cultured dermal papilla cells. At the highest concentration, markers of cell death pointed in the direction of fewer apoptotic papilla cells, although the reduction in apoptotic cell counts was not statistically significant. The authors proposed that AHK-Cu promotes follicle growth by stimulating papilla cell proliferation and limiting apoptosis.[1] No human trial of AHK-Cu for hair growth was found.

paras: AHK-Cu is related to GHK-Cu, a copper complex of glycyl-histidyl-lysine that Loren Pickart (1938-2023) is credited with isolating from human plasma albumin in 1973; the factor was identified as glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine in 1977.[2] GHK-Cu is widely used in anti-aging and hair-loss-prevention products as copper tripeptide-1; Wikipedia describes controlled facial studies reporting anti-aging, firming and anti-wrinkle effects, but with small samples and short durations.[2] Wikipedia's GHK-Cu article lists AHK-Cu only as a related topic and gives no description of it.[2]

The 2007 study evaluated L-alanyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine-Cu2+ on human hair growth ex vivo and on cultured dermal papilla cells. Dermal papilla cells are specialised fibroblasts important in hair follicle morphogenesis and growth. AHK-Cu stimulated elongation of human hair follicles ex vivo and proliferation of the papilla cells, and at the highest concentration raised the Bcl-2/Bax ratio and lowered levels of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP, changes the authors read as limiting apoptosis.[1] The study's introduction notes that tripeptide-copper complexes stimulate dermal fibroblast proliferation and raise vascular endothelial growth factor production while lowering transforming growth factor-beta1 secretion.[1]

No human trials of AHK-Cu for hair were found. The published evidence is the 2007 ex vivo and cell-culture study described above.[1] A registered early phase 1 trial of systemic and topical interventions assessed with aging clocks (NCT07888595) was listed as enrolling by invitation; its relevance to hair outcomes is not established.[3]

timeline.event: Loren Pickart isolates GHK-Cu from human plasma albumin.[2]
The factor is identified as glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine.[2]
Ex vivo and cell-culture study reports AHK-Cu stimulates hair follicle elongation and papilla cell proliferation.[1]
